title: Notes from Underground
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
summary: Em São Petersburgo, um ex-funcionário público amargo e solitário se esconde do mundo no seu “subsolo” e escreve uma confissão cheia de raiva, ironia e ideias provocadoras sobre a consciência, o rancor e a liberdade humana contra a razão. Depois, ele relembra episódios humilhantes da sua juventude: a obsessão por um oficial que o ignorou, um jantar desastroso com antigos colegas de escola e o encontro com Liza, uma jovem que talvez pudesse salvá-lo de si mesmo.

chapters.title: Part One: A Sick and Spiteful Man
paragraphs: I am a sick man. I am a spiteful man. I am an unattractive man. I believe there is something wrong with my liver. However, I know nothing at all about my illness, and I am not even sure what is hurting me. I refuse to see a doctor, although I respect medicine and doctors. I refuse out of spite. You probably will not understand that. Well, I understand it.

I have been living like this for a long time, for about twenty years. I am forty now. I used to work in the government service, but I am not working any more. I was a spiteful official. I was rude to people, and I enjoyed being rude. When people came to my desk to ask for something, I ground my teeth at them. When I managed to make one of them unhappy, I felt real pleasure.

But do you know the worst thing? Even at the moment of my greatest anger, I knew, to my shame, that I was not really a spiteful man at all. I was only frightening sparrows and amusing myself. If someone had brought me a doll to play with, or a cup of sweet tea, I would probably have calmed down at once. I would even have been touched. Later, of course, I would have gnashed my teeth at myself and been unable to sleep for months out of shame. That is how I am.

I lied just now when I said I was a spiteful official. I lied out of spite. In fact, I could never become anything at all. I could not become spiteful, or kind, or a scoundrel, or an honest man, or a hero, or even an insect. And now I am living out my life in my corner, comforting myself with the bitter thought that an intelligent man cannot seriously become anything. Only a fool becomes something. A man of the nineteenth century must be a creature without character. A man of character, a man of action, is limited by nature. That is my belief at forty.

Who am I? I was a collegiate assessor, a minor official. I worked in order to eat. When a distant relative left me six thousand roubles in his will last year, I resigned immediately and moved into my corner. I lived in this corner before, but now I have settled in it for good. My room is miserable and ugly, on the edge of the city. My servant is an old village woman, stupid and bad-tempered, and she smells unpleasant. People tell me that the climate of St Petersburg is bad for me, and that life here is expensive with my small income. I know all that better than all these wise advisers. But I am staying in St Petersburg. I will not leave. Why will I not leave? Oh, it really does not matter whether I leave or not.

Now, gentlemen, I want to tell you, whether you want to hear it or not, why I could not even become an insect. I tell you seriously that I have many times tried to become an insect. But I did not even deserve that. I swear to you, gentlemen, that to be too conscious is an illness, a real, complete illness. For ordinary human life, an ordinary amount of consciousness would be more than enough. Half, or even a quarter, of the consciousness of a cultivated man of our unhappy century would be plenty.

You are laughing at me, perhaps. Laugh, then. I am not offended. I know that I am talking nonsense. But tell me: why did it always happen that at the very moment when I was most able to feel all the beauty of “the good and the beautiful”, as people used to say, I did the ugliest things? The more conscious I was of goodness, the deeper I sank into the mud. And the strangest part was this. It did not feel like an accident. It felt as though this was my normal state, and in the end I lost all wish to fight against it.

chapters.title: Part One: The Mouse and the Stone Wall
paragraphs: Let me explain my strange pleasure. I would come home on some disgusting St Petersburg night, after doing something shameful, and I would be fully aware that I had done something shameful again. Then I would secretly bite myself for it, tear myself apart, until the bitterness turned into a kind of shameful sweetness, and finally into real, serious pleasure. Yes, pleasure! The pleasure came from feeling my own humiliation so clearly. It came from knowing that I had reached the last wall, that it was horrible, but that it could not be otherwise.

Now let us look at the man of action. How does he take revenge? When such a man wants revenge, he simply rushes towards his goal like an angry bull, with his horns down. Only a wall can stop him. And before a wall, these simple people give up at once. For them, a wall is not an excuse to turn back, as it is for us thinking people. It is something calming, something final, almost mystical. I envy such a man with all my heart. He is stupid, I do not argue with that. But perhaps a normal man ought to be stupid.

Now look at the opposite: a man of acute consciousness. He is like a mouse. A mouse, I say, not a man. And this mouse has also been insulted, and it also wants revenge. But around the original insult it builds so many doubts and questions that it cannot move. It asks itself whether it has the right to revenge, whether revenge is just, whether it will look ridiculous. And then the miserable mouse goes back into its hole under the floor. There, in its cold, poisonous, eternal spite, it remembers the insult for forty years, adding new details each time, inventing new humiliations to torment itself with.

It is in this cold, horrible half-despair, half-belief, in this conscious burying of yourself alive in the underground for forty years, that the strange pleasure I spoke of is found. People with strong nerves will not understand this at all. “Maybe,” you will say, “people who have never had a slap in the face will not understand it either.” And you will hint politely that I myself have had a slap in the face, and that I am speaking as an expert. I bet that is what you are thinking. But calm yourselves, gentlemen. I have not had one, though I do not care what you think.

Now, what about the stone wall? What wall? The laws of nature, of course, the conclusions of the natural sciences and of mathematics. When they prove to you, for example, that you are descended from a monkey, it is no use frowning. You must accept it. When they prove to you that one drop of your own fat must really be dearer to you than a hundred thousand of your fellow men, you must accept that too. “Excuse me,” they will shout, “you cannot protest. This is two times two makes four! Nature does not ask your permission.”

Good heavens, what do I care about the laws of nature and arithmetic, when for some reason I do not like these laws, and I do not like two times two makes four? Of course I cannot break through such a wall with my head if I really do not have the strength. But I will not accept it just because it is a stone wall and I am weak.

Take a toothache, for example. You will laugh, but there is pleasure even in a toothache. A man with toothache does not suffer in silence. He moans. But these moans are not honest. They are full of spite. They express the whole humiliating meaninglessness of the pain. The man knows that nobody is guilty, that there is no one to punish, and that the pain will go on anyway. And so, after a while, he begins to moan in a nasty, cruel way, for days and nights, to disturb his family. He knows perfectly well that he is only annoying them, and that he could stop moaning. And that is exactly where his pleasure lies.

Well, can a man who finds pleasure even in his own humiliation respect himself at all? I have no regret about it, you understand. Still, I could never bear to say, “Forgive me, Papa, I will not do it again.” It was not that I was unable to say it. On the contrary, I said it far too often, and with deep feeling. That is the trouble. I was always lying, even when I cried real tears.

chapters.title: Part One: Against Reason
paragraphs: Tell me, gentlemen, who was the first to announce that man does nasty things only because he does not know his own real interests? They say that if you enlighten him, if you open his eyes to his true advantage, he will immediately stop doing nasty things. He will become good and noble, because he will see that his advantage lies in goodness. Nobody, they say, can knowingly act against his own interest. Oh, what a sweet, innocent baby the man who said this must have been!

Let us look at history. How many times have millions of people, knowing perfectly well where their real advantage lay, pushed it aside and rushed down another road, a dangerous road, into the dark? Nobody forced them. They simply did not want the sensible path. They preferred to make a difficult, absurd road for themselves. It seems that this stubbornness was more pleasant to them than any advantage.

And what is advantage, anyway? Can you define exactly what it consists of? What if a man's advantage sometimes lies precisely in wishing for something harmful, rather than something useful? I am not joking. Your scientists make lists of human advantages, using averages and statistics: wealth, freedom, peace, comfort. But they always forget one advantage, the most important of all, which does not fit into any list. If you put it in, the whole list falls apart.

Now they tell us that science will soon discover all the laws of nature, and that then man will no longer be responsible for his actions. Everything will be calculated mathematically, like a table of logarithms, up to 108,000, and printed in a book. Every action will be listed in advance, like in a calendar. There will be no more adventures in the world, and no more crimes. Then, they say, new economic relations will be established, ready-made and calculated with mathematical exactness, and all possible questions will vanish in an instant, because all possible answers will be provided.

Of course, nobody can promise that it will not be terribly boring then. But what will people not think of out of boredom? I would not be at all surprised if, in the middle of this future reasonable world, some gentleman suddenly appeared, with an ungrateful, mocking face. He would put his hands on his hips and say to all of us: “Well, gentlemen, why don't we kick this whole reasonable system to pieces, send these logarithms to the devil, and live again according to our own stupid will?” And he would certainly find followers. That is how man is made.

And all this for the most foolish reason. Man, whoever he is, has always liked to act as he chooses, not as reason and advantage tell him. A man can choose something against his own interest, and sometimes he absolutely must. One's own free choice, one's own wish, however wild, one's own fancy, even if it is driven to madness, that is the forgotten advantage, the one that does not fit into any list. Man only needs independent wishes, whatever they cost and wherever they lead.

“But wishes can also be calculated,” you will say. “Science will one day find the formula for all our wishes.” Well, if that happens, man will stop wishing. What is the pleasure in wishing according to a table? Man would become a piano key, an organ stop played by the laws of nature. And even if he really were nothing but a piano key, even if it were proven to him mathematically, he would still do something out of pure ingratitude, just to prove that he is a man and not a piano key. If he could find no other way, he would invent destruction and chaos. He would curse the world. Perhaps he would go mad on purpose, simply to be free of reason and to have his own way.

You will shout at me that nobody is taking away my free will, that they are only trying to arrange things so that my will agrees with my real interests. But, gentlemen, what kind of free will is that, when everything comes down to tables and arithmetic, when only two times two makes four is allowed? Two times two will make four without my will. Is that what you call free will?

chapters.title: Part One: The Crystal Palace
paragraphs: Man is a creature who loves to build, that cannot be denied. He loves to build roads into the future. But why does he also love destruction and chaos so passionately? Perhaps it is because he is instinctively afraid of reaching his goal and finishing the building. Perhaps he loves the building only from a distance, not up close. Perhaps he likes the process of reaching a goal, not the goal itself. Who knows? Two times two makes four is no longer life, gentlemen. It is the beginning of death.

And why are you so sure that man wants only what is good for him? Perhaps he loves suffering just as much as comfort. Sometimes man loves suffering terribly, passionately. That is a fact. I am not saying suffering is good, or comfort is good. I am in favour of my own wish, and of having it when I need it. Suffering, after all, is the only source of consciousness. And consciousness, though I said at the beginning that it is man's greatest misfortune, is something he would never exchange for any satisfaction.

You believe in a Crystal Palace, a great building of glass and iron that can never be destroyed. It is the perfect, reasonable society of the future, where everyone is happy and everything is calculated. Nobody will be able to stick out his tongue at it, or make a rude gesture at it in secret. Well, perhaps that is exactly why I am afraid of this building. I do not want to live in a palace where I am not allowed to stick out my tongue.

You see, if instead of a palace there were only a chicken coop, and it started to rain, I might climb into the chicken coop to stay dry. But I would not call the chicken coop a palace just because it kept me out of the rain. You laugh and say that in that case a chicken coop and a palace are the same thing. Yes, if we live only in order to keep out of the rain. But what if I have decided that we do not live only for that? Show me something better, and I will follow you. Until then, I will not accept a chicken coop as a palace, and I will not accept a block of flats for poor people with a thousand-year lease as the crown of my desires.

Well, gentlemen, the conclusion is this: it is better to do nothing at all! Conscious inertia is better. So, long live the underground! I said that I envied the normal man. But I would not want to be him, not if I had to live in the conditions in which I see him. Although, I am lying. I am lying because I know myself, like two times two, that the underground is not better at all. It is something different, something I long for and cannot find. To the devil with the underground!

You will ask me why I am writing all this, if I do not even believe what I say. And who are these “gentlemen” I keep talking to? I am writing for myself, of course. I only pretend to talk to readers because it is easier that way. I will never have any readers. But there are memories in every man's life that he does not tell anybody, except perhaps his friends. There are others that he will not even tell his friends, only himself, and in secret. And there are others, finally, that he is afraid to tell even himself.

Recently I remembered one such event from long ago, and it has been bothering me ever since. Perhaps if I write it down, I will be free of it. Today it is snowing, a wet, yellow, dirty snow. Yesterday it was snowing too, and the day before. I think it was the wet snow that reminded me of the story I cannot get out of my head. So let it be a story about the wet snow.

chapters.title: Part Two: The Officer in the Tavern
paragraphs: At that time I was only twenty-four. My life even then was gloomy, disordered and lonely to the point of savagery. I made friends with nobody and avoided talking to people. I buried myself more and more in my corner. At work in the office I tried never to look at anybody, and I noticed very well that my colleagues considered me a strange person, and even looked at me with disgust. I hated them all, and at the same time I was afraid of them. Sometimes I thought I was cleverer than all of them, and sometimes I felt lower than all of them.

At home I spent most of my time reading. I wanted to drown everything that was boiling inside me with impressions from outside. But reading was not enough, and sometimes I felt a terrible need to do something. Then I would sink into dark, secret, shameful little adventures at night. I went out alone, in the dark, hiding, with a nervous feeling of shame that never left me. I was already carrying the underground inside my soul.

One night, as I was passing a small tavern, I saw through the lighted window some gentlemen fighting with billiard cues. One of them was thrown out of the window. At another time I would have felt disgusted. But at that moment I envied the man who had been thrown out of the window. I envied him so much that I even went into the tavern and into the billiard room. “Perhaps,” I thought, “I will get into a fight too, and they will throw me out of the window.”

I was not drunk, but what can you expect? Depression can drive a man to such hysteria. But nothing happened. It turned out that I was not even fit to be thrown out of a window, and I went away without having had my fight.

As I stood near the billiard table, blocking the way without realizing it, an officer needed to pass. He was a very tall man. He took me by the shoulders and, without a word, without any warning or explanation, moved me from where I was standing to another place. Then he passed by as if he had not noticed me at all. I could have forgiven him if he had hit me. But I could not forgive him for moving me like a piece of furniture, as if I were a fly.

The devil knows what I would have given for a real, proper quarrel, a more decent, more literary one. But I had been treated like a fly. The officer was tall, and I was short and thin. But the quarrel was in my hands. I only had to protest, and they certainly would have thrown me out of the window. But I changed my mind and preferred to slip away, full of resentment.

Do not think I was a coward because I was afraid of him. I have never been a coward at heart, though I have always been a coward in action. Do not laugh, there is an explanation. I was not afraid of being beaten. I was afraid that nobody in the room would understand my protest. I was sure that if I had begun to talk about a point of honour, not in the street language but in literary language, they would all have laughed at me. The officer would not simply have beaten me. He would have kicked me around the billiard table, and only then, perhaps, thrown me out of the window.

So I left the tavern, confused and troubled. The next night I went back to my little adventures, more timidly, more gloomily than before, as though there were tears in my eyes. But I did go on with them. And do not think that I forgot the officer. I thought about him constantly for years afterwards. My resentment grew with every year.

I began by finding out everything about him. I followed him in the street from a distance, as if I were tied to him. Once I heard someone shout his name, and so I learned what he was called. Another time I followed him home and found out where he lived and what floor he lived on. Then I had an idea. One morning, although I had never written anything for publication, I decided to write a story about him. I made him the villain, and I gave him a name so similar to his real name that anyone could guess it. I sent it to a magazine. But stories like that were not fashionable any more, and they did not print it. I was terribly disappointed.

chapters.title: Part Two: The Bump on Nevsky Prospect
paragraphs: Sometimes I felt the urge to challenge him to a duel. I even wrote him a beautiful, charming letter, begging him to apologize to me, and hinting quite clearly that I would fight a duel if he refused. The letter was written in such a way that, if the officer had understood anything at all about “the good and the beautiful”, he would certainly have run to me, thrown his arms around my neck and offered me his friendship. And how wonderful that would have been! We would have lived together so happily. Fortunately, I never sent the letter. When I think of it now, a cold shiver runs down my back.

Then suddenly, two years after the insult, I found a way to take revenge, the simplest way, a stroke of genius. On holidays I sometimes walked along the Nevsky Prospect, the most fashionable street in the city, on the sunny side, at about four o'clock. Or rather, I did not walk. I suffered a series of humiliations. I wriggled like an eel among the people, constantly stepping aside for generals, for officers of the guards, for ladies. At those moments I felt like a fly in the eyes of the whole world, a nasty, useless fly.

The officer also walked on the Nevsky, very often. I watched him. He too stepped aside for generals and important people, and he too wriggled between them like an eel. But for people like me, even for people a little better dressed than me, he simply went straight ahead. He walked towards them as if there were empty space in front of him, and under no circumstances did he ever step aside.

I would meet him and step aside, every single time, and I would feel sick with anger. “Why must I always be the first to step aside?” I asked myself, waking up at night in a fury. “Why is it me and not him? There is no law about it. Why can we not meet as equals, each of us stepping aside a little, as polite people do?” And then the brilliant idea came to me. “What if I do not step aside? What if I do not step aside on purpose, even if I have to bump into him? How would that be?”

This bold idea took control of me. I dreamed about it all the time. I went to the Nevsky more often, so that I could imagine it more clearly. But first I had to prepare. My clothes were shabby and old. I had to look decent when we collided, so that people would see I was a gentleman. I needed new gloves and a decent hat. And my old coat, with its cheap raccoon collar, would not do at all. I needed a beaver collar, like an officer's.

To buy it I had to borrow money from the head of my department, Anton Antonich Setochkin, a serious and calm man who had never lent money to anybody. I asked him, trembling, for a loan against my next salary. He looked at me in surprise, but he lent it to me. I bought the collar. I was ready.

But it was not so easy. The first time I planned to do it, at the last moment, when we were only a few steps apart, I lost my nerve and stepped aside, and he passed by without noticing me. The same thing happened again and again. Once I finally decided to do it, and I closed my eyes, but at the last second I jumped aside and fell at his feet. That night I was ill with fever. My plan seemed hopeless.

And then, suddenly, everything happened in the most wonderful way. The night before, I had decided to give up my fatal plan, and I had gone to the Nevsky just to see how I would give it up. Suddenly, three steps from my enemy, I made up my mind without thinking. I closed my eyes, and we bumped hard, shoulder against shoulder! I did not move an inch. I passed by him as an equal! He did not even look round, and he pretended not to notice. But I am sure he only pretended. I am sure of it even now.

Of course, I got the worst of it, because he was stronger. But that was not the point. The point was that I had achieved my aim. I had kept up my dignity, I had not stepped aside, and I had publicly placed myself on an equal social footing with him. I came home feeling completely avenged. I was delighted. I sang Italian songs. A few days later he was transferred somewhere, and I have not seen him for fourteen years.

chapters.title: Part Two: An Unwanted Guest
paragraphs: After my little adventures I used to escape into dreams. I dreamed terribly, for three months at a time, hidden in my corner. In my dreams I was always a hero. I triumphed over everyone. Everybody, of course, was lying in the dust at my feet and was forced to admire my perfection, and I forgave them all. I fell in love, I became a famous poet, I gave away millions to humanity. These dreams were sweet, but after a few months of them I always felt an irresistible need to rush into society, to embrace real people.

Rushing into society meant, for me, visiting my only acquaintance, my former schoolfellow Simonov. One evening in winter, at about eight o'clock, I climbed the stairs to his fourth-floor flat. I had not seen him for about a year.

I found two other old schoolfellows with him. They seemed to be discussing something important. They hardly noticed my arrival, which was strange, since we had not seen each other for years. Evidently they looked on me as some sort of ordinary fly. Even at school they had never treated me like that, though they had all hated me.

I soon understood what they were discussing. They were planning a farewell dinner for another old schoolfellow, Zverkov, an officer who was leaving for a distant province. Zverkov had been at school with all of us. I had particularly hated him in the upper classes. As a boy he had been a pretty, playful child whom everybody liked. He had always been a bad student, but he had passed his exams through his connections. In our last year at school he had inherited a large estate, and he had begun to boast loudly to all of us about his money and his future successes with women.

“So, seven roubles each,” said Trudolyubov, a tall, cold young man who worshipped success. “Three of us, that makes twenty-one roubles. We can have a good dinner for that. Zverkov will not pay, of course. He is our guest.”
“And the dinner is at five o'clock tomorrow, at the Hôtel de Paris,” said Ferfichkin, a small man with a face like a monkey, who had been my bitterest enemy since our early school days.
Then, suddenly, I heard myself say: “And what about me? Count me in. Then it will be twenty-eight roubles.”
They all looked at me in astonishment. They knew perfectly well that Zverkov and I could not stand each other.
“You?” said Ferfichkin rudely. “But you were never friends with Zverkov.”
“How can you judge that?” I answered, my voice trembling. “Perhaps that is exactly why I want to come now, because I was not his friend before.”
“Well, it is up to you,” said Trudolyubov with disgust. “Only, it is a private party, for friends.”

“We are all friends here,” I said, and I could not stop myself. Simonov, embarrassed, agreed that I could come. When I left, he reminded me coldly that I already owed him fifteen roubles. “I mention it only because...” he began. I interrupted him and said I would pay him back tomorrow, at the dinner.

I went home furious with myself. Why had I pushed myself into this dinner? I hated them all. I did not even have the money. I had to pay my servant, Apollon, his wages, and that took all I had. Apollon was a terrible man, the pest of my existence. He was proud, pompous and silent, and he looked at me with endless contempt. He was always reading psalms in a low, monotonous voice behind his partition, and he despised me, I am sure of it. I could not get rid of him. It was as if he were part of my flat, part of my life.

All night I dreamed of the dinner. In my head, I would arrive, and they would see how superior I was, how intelligent, how witty. I would humiliate Zverkov with my brilliant conversation, and then I would forgive him. Then, in the morning, I woke up and realized how ridiculous it all was. “I will not go,” I thought. And of course I knew that I would go. Nothing in the world could have stopped me.

chapters.title: Part Two: The Dinner with Zverkov
paragraphs: I arrived at the Hôtel de Paris at exactly five o'clock. Nobody was there. The waiter told me that the table had been ordered for six. They had changed the time and had not told me. I had to wait an hour, alone, in front of the waiter, who looked at me with pity. I felt that everyone in the restaurant was laughing at me.

At six o'clock they finally arrived, all together, with Zverkov at their head. He came in like a general, smiling and confident. He held out his hand to me in a friendly but slightly superior way, as if he were doing me a favour.
“I have heard you wanted to join us,” he said in a kind voice. “I was surprised, but I am glad. Why are you always so serious? Do not be afraid of us.”
“Oh, did they tell you I would come at five?” I said, red with anger. “Nobody told me you had changed the time.”

“They did not tell you?” said Zverkov, turning to Simonov. Simonov only shrugged. They all laughed, and they did not apologize at all. We sat down. They began to ask me questions, with mock politeness, about my job and my salary.

“And how much do you earn?” asked Zverkov. I told him. “That is very little,” he said, with pity. “But you have become so thin! Your clothes are not very good either.” Ferfichkin laughed loudly. I could feel my face burning.
“Gentlemen,” I said in a loud voice, “I am not dining here to be insulted. My salary is nobody's business.”
“Dining?” said Ferfichkin. “You are not dining at somebody else's expense, I hope?”

Then they turned away from me and began to talk among themselves. Zverkov told stories about a princess who had fallen in love with him, and about his duels and his horses. They all laughed at his jokes. I drank glass after glass of wine and felt more and more humiliated.
When they began to make speeches in honour of Zverkov, I suddenly stood up with a glass in my hand.

“Gentlemen,” I said, “I also want to propose a toast. Mr Zverkov, I hate empty phrases and people who boast about their success with women. I hate people who wear tight waists. I drink to truth, to sincerity and to honesty. And I drink to your health, Mr Zverkov. Charm the women, shoot the enemies, and...”
Zverkov stood up, bowed to me and said, “I am very much obliged to you.” He was offended and had turned pale.
“He should be punched in the face for this!” shouted Ferfichkin.
“I demand satisfaction!” I cried. “Tomorrow we will fight a duel!”
“A duel? With you?” said Ferfichkin. They all burst out laughing. After that, they ignored me completely. They moved to the sofa and continued talking and laughing, as though I did not exist.

What could I do? I could have left. But I did not. Out of pure spite I stayed, and for three hours I walked up and down the room, from the table to the stove and from the stove back to the table, with my boots making a loud noise. I wanted to show them that I could manage without them. But they paid no attention to me. Sometimes Zverkov looked at me with cold contempt, and I felt that I was the lowest of men.
At eleven o'clock they decided to go somewhere else, to a certain house of bad reputation. As they were leaving, I ran up to Zverkov.
“Zverkov, I ask your forgiveness,” I said. “I insulted you. Please forgive me.”
“Forgive you?” he said, looking down at me. “You could never insult me.”
Then I turned to Simonov, desperate. “Simonov, lend me six roubles,” I said.
He looked at me in astonishment. “Are you really coming with us?” he asked.
“Yes,” I said. He threw the money on the table and walked out. They were gone.

chapters.title: Part Two: Liza
paragraphs: I stood alone in the room, among the dirty plates and broken glasses. My head was spinning. “So this is it,” I thought. “This is my meeting with reality.” Then I rushed downstairs, took a sledge and told the driver to follow them. The wet snow was falling in large flakes.

On the way, I made terrible plans. “I will go in and slap Zverkov in the face,” I thought. “They will throw me out, but I will have slapped him. Then he will have to fight a duel with me. Or I will wait for him in the street and bite his hand. Then I will be sent to prison, to Siberia, and fifteen years later I will come back, a poor beggar, and find him. I will say to him, ‘Look at me. I have lost everything because of you. But I forgive you.’ And then I will fire my pistol into the air.” I almost wept with emotion as I imagined it. I knew that it was all taken from books, from Pushkin and Lermontov, but I could not stop.
When I arrived, they were not there. They had gone somewhere else. I felt, strangely, almost relieved. I walked into the house anyway and went into a room with a girl.

Much later, I woke up in the dark. A candle was burning low on the table. I realized that I was not alone. Two wide-open eyes were looking at me curiously and steadily. The look was cold, distant and indifferent, and it made me feel sick. A girl was lying next to me. A gloomy thought came into my head, a nasty sensation, like walking into a damp, cold cellar.
“What is your name?” I asked sharply, to end the silence.
“Liza,” she whispered, not very politely, and turned her eyes away.
“Where are you from?”
“From Riga,” she said reluctantly.
“How old are you?”
“Twenty.”

I was silent for a while. Then I said: “Today, in the morning, I saw a coffin. They were carrying it out of a house near the Haymarket. It was a girl's coffin. She had lived in a house like this one. They dropped it in the snow.”
“They dropped it?” she said.

“Yes, in the wet snow. They were carrying it up from the cellar. The men were swearing and joking. She had died of consumption, they said. Nobody was sorry. The grave will be wet, full of water. They will throw her into it and cover her with mud.”
“Why water?” she asked, with some curiosity, but more harshly than before.
“Because the ground there is always wet. Do you think it does not matter? It is not a good thing to die like that.”
“Why do you tell me this?” she said. “What does it matter to me? Everybody dies.”

“Yes, everybody dies. But do you think you will always stay young and fresh? You are young now, you are pretty, they pay for you. But in a year you will be worth less, and they will send you to a worse house. In another year, a worse one still. And in seven years you will be in a cellar near the Haymarket. And then you will die, like that girl, and nobody will even remember you.”

She did not answer. I felt that my words were beginning to have an effect, and I was pleased. It was a kind of game. I wanted to play with her soul, to see what I could do. I had read many books, and I knew how to talk.

chapters.title: Part Two: Pictures of Another Life
paragraphs: “Do you not have a father and mother?” I asked.
“What does it matter to you?” she answered. But after a moment she added: “I have.”

“And they sold you, perhaps?” I said. “Or you ran away from them? Listen, Liza. If I had had a family when I was a child, I would not be what I am now. I often think about it. However bad a family is, your mother and father are still yours. They are not your enemies.”
“Some parents are glad to sell their daughter,” she said quietly.

So that was it, I thought. Something had happened at home. Then I began to paint pictures for her, pictures of a happy family life. I spoke about a young husband and wife who love each other. I described how they quarrel sometimes and make it up again, and how much sweeter love is after a quarrel. I described the first child, and the mother holding the baby, and the father coming home in the evening to his wife and children.

“Who does not love such a life?” I said. “But here, what love can you find? They buy you. And love cannot be bought. A girl who is free can give her love to anyone she chooses. But here you are a slave. You have even given away your soul, and you do not own it any more. Do you understand that?”

I spoke for a long time, with feeling and with great skill. I could feel my own words. I had become carried away. At first I had been playing a game, but soon I was speaking sincerely. Everything I said came out of books, and yet I believed it. Suddenly I noticed that the girl was lying face down with her head in the pillow. Her whole body was shaking with sobs. I had won. I had turned her soul upside down.
I became frightened. I quickly lit another candle and began to dress.
“Liza, my dear,” I said, “I should not have spoken like that. Forgive me.”

She sat up. Her face was pale, and she looked at me with a strange, half-ashamed smile. Then she jumped up and ran to a corner of the room. She came back with a small piece of paper and gave it to me. It was a love letter from a medical student, a young man who had met her at a dance at a respectable family's house. He had not known what she was. He wrote to her with respect, as to an honest girl. She had kept this letter like a treasure. She wanted me to know that someone had once loved her honestly, that she was not only what I saw.
I did not know what to say. I gave the letter back to her.
“Listen, Liza,” I said, “come and see me.” I wrote my address on a piece of paper and gave it to her. “Come,” I repeated. Then I left.

I walked home through the snow. My heart was heavy. Over the next few days I could not stop thinking about her. At first I was proud of myself. But then I began to feel horrified. “What if she comes?” I thought. “She will see how poor I am, how I live, my miserable room, my torn dressing gown, my horrible servant Apollon. She will see that I am a fraud, that I am nothing.” And I was right to be afraid.

chapters.title: Part Two: Liza Comes
paragraphs: For several days I hardly went out. Every evening I waited for her and trembled. Every knock at the door made me jump. “She will come,” I thought. “And what then?” Sometimes I imagined that I was her saviour. I would educate her, teach her to read good books, and she would fall in love with me. She would throw herself at my feet and say, “You saved me.” But then I would think of my dirty room, and I would feel sick with shame.

At that same time I was having a war with Apollon. I had decided not to pay him his wages on the day they were due, to punish him for his pride. He knew what I was doing, and his response was terrible. He would come into my room, stand in front of me in silence and stare at me with an expression of deep contempt. Then he would turn round slowly and leave. Ten minutes later he would come in again and do the same. He did it again and again, until I could not bear it any longer.
On the fourth evening I shouted at him. “What do you want? Get out!” He did not move. He stood there calmly, looking at me. “You have to pay me my wages,” he said finally, in his slow, solemn voice.

“I will not pay you a penny! Not until you come and ask me respectfully!” I cried. “Do you hear me? You are a torturer!” I was shaking, my voice had gone high and strange. He simply went behind his partition and began to read his psalms again.
At that very moment, the door opened quietly, and Liza came in.

She stood at the door, looking at me in my old, torn dressing gown, at my shaking hands and my red face. I wanted to die. I sat down on the sofa, unable to speak. After a moment I jumped up, ran to Apollon and pushed the money into his hand. “Here! Take it! And bring us some tea!” I shouted.
Apollon looked at the money, then at Liza, then at me. Slowly, without a word, he went out. I sat down again, and we were silent. Liza sat on a chair, looking at the floor.
“You have found me in a very difficult situation, Liza,” I said at last, angrily. “Why are you looking at me like that?”
“I have left that house,” she said quietly. “I want to leave it for good.” She was waiting for me to help her, to speak to her again as I had spoken that night.
But a terrible spite rose up inside me. I could not forgive her for having seen me like this, humiliated, in my dressing gown, shouting at my servant. Instead of kindness, I gave her cruelty.

“Why did you come?” I said, laughing. “Do you want to know why I spoke to you like that? I had been humiliated that night by my friends, so I wanted to humiliate someone else. I wanted power. I was laughing at you, Liza. I was playing with you. All those beautiful words were just a game. And now you have seen me in this dressing gown, like a beggar. I will never forgive you for that. Do you understand? I will never forgive you for having seen me!”
I went on and on like this, out of my mind, saying horrible things. I was crying. I had to show her that I was the vilest man in the world. And then something unexpected happened.

Liza, whom I had wanted to humiliate, understood far more than I had imagined. She understood the most important thing, the thing a woman who truly loves always understands first. She understood that I myself was unhappy. A look of fear passed over her face, and then she jumped up from her chair, ran to me and threw her arms around my neck. She burst into tears. I could not hold myself back either, and I sobbed as I had never sobbed before.
“They will not let me... I cannot be good!” I said through my tears. I lay face down on the sofa and cried for a quarter of an hour, in real hysterics, while she held me.

chapters.title: Part Two: The Wet Snow
paragraphs: But the hysterics had to come to an end. When I lifted my head from the sofa, I felt deeply ashamed to look at Liza. And then a strange idea came to me. Our roles had changed completely. She was now the heroine, and I was the humiliated, crushed creature, as she had been that night. And at that thought, a feeling of mastery and possession flashed into my heart. I hated her, and I wanted her at the same time. One feeling made the other stronger. It was almost like revenge.

What happened next I will not describe. A quarter of an hour later I was walking up and down the room in an impatient fury. She was sitting on the floor, in the corner, behind the screen, with her head against the bed. I wanted her to go. I wanted peace. I wanted to be alone in my underground. “Real life” had crushed me with its unfamiliarity, so much that I could hardly breathe.

She came out from behind the screen. She looked at me and understood everything. She understood that I was a man who could not love, that for me love meant to tyrannize and to dominate. She began to put on her coat and her scarf, without speaking.

And then I did something that I will never forget. As she was going out, I ran up to her, took her hand, opened it, put a five-rouble note into it and closed it again. Then I turned away quickly and ran to the other corner of the room, so as not to see.
I did not do it out of my heart. I did it out of my stupid head, out of bookish spite. It was so artificial, so deliberately invented, that I could not keep it up even for a minute.
I heard the door close. She had gone without a word. I stood for a moment, then I looked at the table. The five-rouble note was lying there. She had thrown it down as she left. She had not taken it.

I rushed after her down the dark stairs. “Liza! Liza!” I called, but not loudly. There was no answer. I heard the street door open and close. I ran out into the street without my coat. Everything was silent and white. The snow was falling thickly, almost straight down, covering the pavement and the empty street. There was no one there, not a sound. The street lamps were shining sadly and uselessly through the snow.

I stood there and thought. “Why am I running after her? To fall at her feet, to beg her forgiveness? I would hate her tomorrow, perhaps, just because I had kissed her feet today. Would I make her happy? No. I would torture her.” And I stood in the snow, staring into the misty darkness, and thought of her going home with that humiliation in her soul.

Perhaps, I told myself, it is better this way. Perhaps the insult will purify her. It will be an eternal memory for her, and through hatred she will rise higher. But I did not believe it then, and I do not believe it now. I never saw Liza again, and I never heard anything about her.

I am ashamed to write all this. This is not literature. It is a punishment. Even now, so many years later, all this is very evil in my memory. We have all become unused to real life, gentlemen, every one of us. We even feel a kind of disgust for it, and we prefer to live out of books. We do not even know where real life is, what it is, or what it is called. Leave us alone without books, and we will immediately be lost. As for me, I have only carried to an extreme in my life what you have not dared to carry even halfway. Well, enough. I do not want to write any more from the underground. And here, I think, I can stop.
